title: Enterprise Switching: MAC Learning, VLANs, 802.1Q Trunks, VTP, Spanning Tree, and EtherChannel
intro: Layer 2 switching is how enterprise switches forward Ethernet frames inside a building, using MAC address learning, VLAN segmentation, trunk links, loop prevention with Spanning Tree, and link bundling. By the end of this lesson you will be able to configure and verify each of these features with real IOS commands, read the show output, and diagnose a VLAN and trunk mismatch step by step.

sections.heading: How a Switch Forwards Frames: MAC Learning, Flooding, and Broadcast Domains
sections.content:
A switch is a Layer 2 device that forwards Ethernet frames using the destination MAC address. A hub repeats every signal out every port. A switch behaves like a mail-room clerk who learns which desk each employee sits at by reading the return address on every envelope, then carries mail only to the right desk. (Frame structure belongs to the OSI lesson. Here we only need the fact that every frame carries a source and a destination MAC.)

**The forwarding algorithm.** Every received frame triggers a learn step and a forward step:

1. **Learn.** The switch records the frame's source MAC, the ingress port, and the VLAN in its MAC address table (also called the CAM table). Entries age out after 300 seconds of silence by default.
2. **Known unicast.** If the destination MAC is in the table for that VLAN, the frame leaves only through that port. If the table says the destination lives on the ingress port itself, the frame is filtered (dropped).
3. **Unknown unicast.** If the destination is not in the table, the switch floods the frame out every port in the same VLAN except the one it arrived on. When the real owner replies, the switch learns it and later frames are sent as plain unicast.
4. **Broadcast and multicast.** Frames to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF are always flooded within the VLAN. Multicast is flooded too unless IGMP snooping limits it to interested ports.

```
Switch# show mac address-table dynamic
          Mac Address Table
-------------------------------------------
Vlan    Mac Address       Type        Ports
----    -----------       --------    -----
  10    0050.7966.6800    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
  10    0050.7966.6801    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
  20    0050.7966.6802    DYNAMIC     Gi0/5
Total Mac Addresses for this criterion: 3
```

The table is keyed by VLAN plus MAC, so the switch keeps an independent table per VLAN.

**Collision domains versus broadcast domains.** Each switch port is its own collision domain, and on full-duplex links collisions no longer occur. The VLAN, however, remains a single broadcast domain: every ARP request and DHCP discover reaches every host in it.

**Why we segment.** Performance: broadcasts interrupt every host CPU. Fault containment: a loop or a broadcast storm stays inside one broadcast domain. Security: users, servers, guests, and phones sit in separate segments. Policy: ACLs and QoS are applied where segments meet at a Layer 3 boundary (subnetting and routing are separate lessons).

**What to know.** The table has finite size. An attacker who floods thousands of fake source MACs can fill it so the switch falls back to flooding, which lets the attacker sniff traffic (port security, section 8, is the control). A loop makes one MAC appear to jump between ports, and the log shows it:

```
%SW_MATM-4-MACFLAP_NOTIF: Host 0050.7966.6800 in vlan 10 is flapping between port Gi0/1 and port Gi0/24
```

**What to ask.** Does the switch know this MAC? On which port? Is that the port I expect for this device? Those three questions drive most Layer 2 troubleshooting.

sections.heading: VLANs and Access Ports
sections.content:
A VLAN (virtual LAN) is a logical broadcast domain defined in the switch rather than by cabling. Analogy: a hotel where floors are fixed in concrete (physical LANs) versus colored key cards that decide which guests can reach which rooms regardless of the floor (VLANs). One physical switch can act as many independent switches, and hosts in different VLANs cannot exchange frames without passing through a Layer 3 device.

**VLAN numbering.** The VLAN ID is a 12-bit field, so the range is 1 to 4094. The normal range 1-1005 is stored in the VLAN database file vlan.dat in flash, not in the running configuration. The extended range 1006-4094 needs VTP transparent mode (or VTP version 3) on most platforms. VLAN 1 is the default and cannot be deleted. VLANs 1002-1005 are legacy FDDI and Token Ring entries that also cannot be deleted.

**Access ports.** An access port belongs to exactly one data VLAN and sends and receives untagged Ethernet frames. The end device (PC, printer, camera) never knows a VLAN exists. The switch assigns the VLAN membership internally as the frame enters.

```
Switch# configure terminal
Switch(config)# vlan 10
Switch(config-vlan)# name SALES
Switch(config-vlan)# vlan 20
Switch(config-vlan)# name ENGINEERING
Switch(config-vlan)# exit
Switch(config)# interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 12
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport mode access
Switch(config-if-range)# switchport access vlan 10
Switch(config-if-range)# end
```

Verify with the command you will use most often in this module:

```
Switch# show vlan brief

VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- -------------------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/13, Gi0/14, Gi0/15
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/2, Gi0/3, Gi0/4
20   ENGINEERING                      active    Gi0/5, Gi0/6
1002 fddi-default                     act/unsup
```

Two details matter. First, trunk ports never appear in show vlan brief, because they do not belong to one VLAN. If a port you expect is missing from the list, check whether it is a trunk. Second, if you assign a port to a VLAN that does not exist, behavior depends on platform and release: some versions create the VLAN automatically, others leave the port inactive. Always confirm with show vlan brief.

**Voice VLANs.** An IP phone usually sits between the switch and a PC, so one physical port carries two VLANs: the PC's untagged data VLAN and the phone's tagged voice VLAN. The switch tells the phone which voice VLAN to tag with using CDP or LLDP-MED.

```
interface GigabitEthernet0/3
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport voice vlan 150
```

**Hygiene.** Do not leave user ports in VLAN 1. Create a dedicated unused parking VLAN, place idle ports there, and shut them down.

**What to ask.** Which VLAN is this port in? Does that VLAN exist and show active on both switches that must carry it? Is the port an access port, or a trunk that only looks like a user port?

sections.heading: Trunking and 802.1Q Tagging
sections.content:
A trunk is a link that carries frames for many VLANs at once, normally between two switches or from a switch to a router or hypervisor. Analogy: a freight truck with a shipping label on every box, so the receiving dock knows which department each box belongs to. IEEE 802.1Q is that label.

**The tag.** 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte field after the source MAC address: a 16-bit TPID with the fixed value 0x8100, a 3-bit priority (PCP, used by QoS), a 1-bit DEI, and a 12-bit VLAN ID. The maximum frame grows from 1518 to 1522 bytes. The receiving switch reads the VID and treats the frame as belonging to that VLAN.

**The native VLAN.** One VLAN on an 802.1Q trunk is sent untagged: the native VLAN, which defaults to VLAN 1. Both ends must agree on it. If switch A sends untagged frames meaning VLAN 1 and switch B treats untagged frames as VLAN 999, traffic leaks from one VLAN into another. Cisco switches warn about the mismatch through CDP:

```
%CDP-4-NATIVE_VLAN_MISMATCH: Native VLAN mismatch discovered on GigabitEthernet0/24 (1), with SW2 GigabitEthernet0/24 (999).
```

Best practice is to set the native VLAN to an unused VLAN on every trunk, which also reduces exposure to double-tagging VLAN hopping attacks.

**Configuring a trunk.**

```
interface GigabitEthernet0/24
 description UPLINK-TO-DIST1
 switchport trunk encapsulation dot1q
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,150
 switchport nonegotiate
```

The encapsulation command is needed only on platforms that also support the obsolete ISL protocol. Newer switches support only dot1q and reject the command.

**The allowed VLAN list.** By default a trunk carries VLANs 1-4094. Limiting it is good hygiene, but it has a classic pitfall: switchport trunk allowed vlan 30 replaces the whole list with just VLAN 30. To modify the list use the keywords add, remove, or except, for example switchport trunk allowed vlan add 30.

**DTP and why we hardcode.** Dynamic Trunking Protocol lets two ports negotiate a trunk. Modes dynamic auto and dynamic desirable are negotiable, and on many Catalyst models the default is dynamic auto. A host that sends DTP frames can talk a user port into becoming a trunk and then receive traffic from every VLAN. Two dynamic auto ports never form a trunk, because neither initiates. The rule is to hardcode every port: mode access on user ports, mode trunk on trunks, and switchport nonegotiate on trunks to stop DTP frames.

```
Switch# show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/24      on           802.1q         trunking      999

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/24      10,20,150

Port        Vlans allowed and active in management domain
Gi0/24      10,20,150

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/24      10,20,150
```

**What to ask.** Is the port really trunking? Do both ends match on native VLAN? Is the VLAN present in each block of the output? A VLAN missing from the second block is not allowed, and one missing from the third is not defined or not forwarding on this switch.

sections.heading: VTP: Keeping VLAN Databases Consistent, and Its Dangers
sections.content:
VLAN Trunking Protocol (VTP) is a Cisco-proprietary protocol that copies the VLAN database from one switch to the others in a VTP domain over trunk links. The idea is convenience: create VLAN 40 once on a server switch and every other switch learns it. The cost is that one wrong move can erase the VLAN configuration of an entire campus.

| Mode | Creates and edits VLANs | Applies received updates | Forwards updates |
|---|---|---|---|
| Server | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Client | No | Yes | Yes |
| Transparent | Local only | No | Yes (v1 and v2) |
| Off | Local only | No | No |

**The revision number.** Each VLAN change on a server increments a 32-bit configuration revision number and advertises the database. A receiving switch in the same domain (matching name and, if set, password) accepts any advertisement whose revision is higher than its own and overwrites its VLAN database completely. It does not merge, and it does not judge which database is more correct. Higher number wins.

**The revision wipe.** Picture a switch taken from a test lab. It has the same domain name, is set to client or server, has revision 85, and holds only VLAN 1 and a couple of lab VLANs. It is plugged into production, where the switches sit at revision 40. The lab database propagates, production switches delete VLANs 10, 20, 150 and the rest, and every access port in those VLANs goes inactive. Users lose connectivity across the building within seconds. Client mode does not protect you, because clients advertise too.

Ways to prevent it:

- Run VTP transparent (or off) everywhere and manage VLANs per switch with automation or templates. Many shops do exactly this.
- If you use VTP, set a password, and prefer VTP version 3, which adds a primary server concept and protects the database from accidental overwrites.
- Before connecting any previously used switch, reset its revision by changing the domain name to a throwaway value and back, or by switching to transparent mode and back.

```
Switch(config)# vtp domain CORP
Switch(config)# vtp mode transparent
Switch(config)# end

Switch# show vtp status
VTP Version running             : 2
VTP Domain Name                 : CORP
VTP Pruning Mode                : Disabled
VTP Operating Mode              : Transparent
Number of existing VLANs        : 7
Configuration Revision          : 0
```

A transparent switch always reports revision 0, so it can never send a bogus higher number.

**VTP pruning.** By default a trunk forwards broadcasts and unknown unicast for every allowed VLAN, even if the far-end switch has no ports in that VLAN. Pruning stops those frames being flooded onto trunks where they are not needed. It is enabled on the server with vtp pruning. A curated switchport trunk allowed vlan list achieves the same result with more control, which is why many designs use transparent mode plus explicit allowed lists.

**What to ask.** What VTP mode and domain is this switch in? What is its revision number? Could any device I am about to connect carry a higher revision?

sections.heading: Spanning Tree Protocol: Loops, Root Bridge, and Port Roles
sections.content:
Spanning Tree Protocol (STP, IEEE 802.1D) prevents Layer 2 loops in networks that have redundant links. Redundancy is essential, since one cable failure should not isolate a building, but Ethernet has no built-in way to stop looping frames.

**The loop problem.** An Ethernet frame has no TTL. If three switches are cabled in a triangle and a broadcast arrives, each switch floods it to the other two, which flood it back, forever. Within seconds a broadcast storm consumes all bandwidth and CPU, MAC tables thrash (the flapping log from section 1), and the network goes down. STP logically blocks some ports so the topology becomes a loop-free tree, while keeping the blocked links ready as backups.

**BPDUs and bridge ID.** Switches exchange Bridge Protocol Data Units (BPDUs), sent by default every 2 seconds. Each switch has a bridge ID made of a priority and its MAC address. Twelve bits of the priority field carry the VLAN ID (extended system ID), so priority is set in steps of 4096. The default is 32768, so VLAN 10 shows as 32778.

**Election and roles.**

1. **Root bridge.** The lowest bridge ID wins. If priorities tie, the lowest MAC wins, which usually means the oldest switch. That is rarely the switch you want, so set the priority deliberately.
2. **Root port.** Every non-root switch picks the one port with the lowest path cost to the root. Typical costs: 100 Mb/s is 19, 1 Gb/s is 4, 10 Gb/s is 2. Ties break on the lowest sender bridge ID, then lowest sender port ID.
3. **Designated port.** On each segment, the port on the switch with the best path to the root forwards toward the root.
4. **Blocked (alternate) port.** Everything else blocks.

| 802.1D state | Learns MACs | Forwards data | Duration |
|---|---|---|---|
| Blocking | No | No | up to 20 s (max age) |
| Listening | No | No | 15 s |
| Learning | Yes | No | 15 s |
| Forwarding | Yes | Yes | stable |
| Disabled | No | No | admin down |

A port coming up in classic STP needs about 30 seconds, and up to 50 seconds after an indirect failure, before it forwards.

**Per-VLAN trees.** Cisco switches run PVST+ (one tree per VLAN) by default. That allows load sharing: be root for some VLANs on one core switch and for the others on the second.

```
Switch(config)# spanning-tree mode rapid-pvst
Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 10,20 root primary
Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 30,40 root secondary
Switch(config)# spanning-tree vlan 50 priority 4096
```

```
Switch# show spanning-tree vlan 10
VLAN0010
  Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
  Root ID    Priority    24586
             Address     0019.e8aa.1100
             Cost        4
             Port        24 (GigabitEthernet0/24)
  Bridge ID  Priority    32778  (priority 32768 sys-id-ext 10)
             Address     0019.e8bb.2200

Interface           Role Sts Cost      Prio.Nbr Type
------------------- ---- --- --------- -------- ---------------
Gi0/23              Altn BLK 4         128.23   P2p
Gi0/24              Root FWD 4         128.24   P2p
```

**What to ask.** Where is the root bridge, and is it the switch I intended? Which ports are blocking, and are they the ones I expect?

sections.heading: PortFast, BPDU Guard, and Rapid Spanning Tree (802.1w)
sections.content:
Classic STP is safe but slow, and it trusts every device that sends a BPDU. Three features fix those weaknesses.

**RSTP (IEEE 802.1w).** Rapid Spanning Tree keeps the same root election but converges in about a second on healthy links instead of 30 to 50 seconds. The main improvements:

- **Fewer states.** Discarding, learning, and forwarding replace blocking, listening, and disabled.
- **New roles.** Alternate (a pre-computed backup for the root port) and backup (a standby for a designated port on a shared segment).
- **Handshake.** On point-to-point full-duplex links, neighbors negotiate with proposal and agreement messages and move to forwarding without waiting for timers.
- **Active keepalive.** Every switch sends its own BPDU each hello interval, and three missed hellos mean the neighbor is gone. In 802.1D only the root originates BPDUs.
- **Edge ports.** Ports connected to end hosts go straight to forwarding.

Cisco rapid-pvst mode is the usual choice. Interoperability with legacy 802.1D switches is automatic but slows those segments down.

**PortFast.** A port facing a PC does not need to wait 30 seconds, because no loop can start behind a single host. PortFast makes the port skip listening and learning and go straight to forwarding. Forgetting it is a classic fault: PCs time out on DHCP during boot, because the link is up but the port is not yet forwarding.

```
interface GigabitEthernet0/5
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
!
spanning-tree portfast default
spanning-tree portfast bpduguard default
errdisable recovery cause bpduguard
errdisable recovery interval 300
```

The global commands apply PortFast and BPDU Guard to all access ports at once. For a server with a trunk to a hypervisor, use spanning-tree portfast trunk. Never enable PortFast on a link to another switch, because it can create a loop that STP no longer prevents.

**BPDU Guard.** PortFast ports should never receive BPDUs. If one does, someone connected a switch (maybe a cheap desk switch with a loop, maybe an attacker advertising a superior bridge ID to become root). BPDU Guard shuts the port down immediately:

```
%SPANTREE-2-BLOCK_BPDUGUARD: Received BPDU on port Gi0/5 with BPDU Guard enabled. Disabling port.
%PM-4-ERR_DISABLE: bpduguard error detected on Gi0/5, putting Gi0/5 in err-disable state
```

To recover, remove the offending device, then shutdown and no shutdown the interface, or let errdisable recovery do it after the timer.

**Root Guard and Loop Guard.** Root Guard on ports facing the access layer refuses to let a switch behind them become root: if a superior BPDU arrives, the port goes root-inconsistent until it stops. Loop Guard protects against a unidirectional link failure, where BPDUs stop arriving but the link looks up, which would otherwise turn a blocked port into a forwarding one.

**What to ask.** Is this an edge port? Does it have PortFast and BPDU Guard? If a port went err-disabled, what device sent the BPDU, and was it supposed to be there?

sections.heading: EtherChannel: Bundling Links with LACP, PAgP, or Static
sections.content:
EtherChannel (link aggregation) bundles several physical links between two devices into one logical Port-channel interface. It increases bandwidth and gives sub-second failover when a member link fails. Analogy: turning four single-lane roads into one four-lane highway with a single name. STP sees one link, so it does not block the extra cables.

| Method | Standard | Modes | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| LACP | IEEE 802.3ad / 802.1AX | active, passive | Works across vendors. Preferred choice. |
| PAgP | Cisco proprietary | desirable, auto | Cisco to Cisco only. |
| Static | none | on | No negotiation, no error detection. |

A bundle forms when at least one side initiates: active with active or passive, desirable with desirable or auto. Passive with passive, or auto with auto, never forms. Mixing protocols (LACP on one side, PAgP on the other) never forms. Mode on pairs only with mode on, and since nothing checks the far end, a miscabled static bundle can create a loop.

**Configuration.** Member ports must have identical settings: speed, duplex, access VLAN or trunk mode, native VLAN, and allowed list. A mismatched port is suspended.

```
interface range GigabitEthernet0/23 - 24
 channel-group 1 mode active
!
interface Port-channel1
 description UPLINK-TO-DIST1
 switchport mode trunk
 switchport trunk native vlan 999
 switchport trunk allowed vlan 10,20,150
!
port-channel load-balance src-dst-ip
```

Configure shared settings on the Port-channel interface, and they propagate to the members. When the bundle is working, the output looks like this:

```
Switch# show etherchannel summary
Flags:  D - down        P - bundled in port-channel
        I - stand-alone s - suspended
        S - Layer2      U - in use
Group  Port-channel  Protocol    Ports
------+-------------+-----------+----------------------------------------
1      Po1(SU)         LACP      Gi0/23(P)   Gi0/24(P)
```

Po1(SU) means a Layer 2 channel that is in use. An (I) or (s) flag beside a member means it is stand-alone or suspended, usually a configuration mismatch or a negotiation failure.

**Load balancing.** The switch hashes selected header fields (source MAC, destination MAC, source IP, destination IP, or combinations) and uses the result to choose a member link. All packets of one flow take the same link, which preserves ordering. Therefore a single large transfer between two hosts uses only one member and never exceeds one link's speed. Four 1 Gb/s links do not make a single TCP stream 4 Gb/s. Choose the hash that spreads your traffic best and check it with show etherchannel load-balance.

**Limits.** A bundle usually allows up to 8 active members (LACP can hold extra standby links). Bundling across two physical switches needs a stacking or multi-chassis technology such as StackWise, VSS, or vPC, which is outside this lesson.

**What to ask.** Which protocol is configured on each side? Are all members bundled (P) or are some suspended? Are member and Port-channel settings identical?

sections.heading: Switch Security Quick Hit: Where These Features Show Up
sections.content:
Every feature in this lesson has a security consequence. This section is a map, not a full treatment. Port-security, DHCP snooping, and Dynamic ARP Inspection have their own lessons, and here we only point out where they connect to what you learned.

| Layer 2 feature | Attack or failure | Typical control |
|---|---|---|
| MAC table (section 1) | MAC flooding fills the CAM table and the switch floods traffic | port-security with a MAC limit per port |
| Access ports (section 2) | Unauthorized device plugged into a wall jack | port-security, 802.1X, shutdown of idle ports |
| Trunks and DTP (section 3) | A host negotiates a trunk and sees all VLANs | switchport mode access, nonegotiate |
| Native VLAN (section 3) | Double-tagging VLAN hopping | unused native VLAN on every trunk |
| VTP (section 4) | Accidental or deliberate VLAN database overwrite | transparent mode, VTP v3, password |
| STP (sections 5-6) | Rogue switch wins the root election and intercepts traffic | BPDU Guard, Root Guard, deliberate priorities |
| Broadcast domain (section 1) | Broadcast and multicast storms | storm-control |

**A hardened access-layer template.** Many commands you have already seen combine into a per-port baseline:

```
interface range GigabitEthernet0/1 - 12
 description USER-PORTS
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 10
 switchport nonegotiate
 spanning-tree portfast
 spanning-tree bpduguard enable
 storm-control broadcast level 5.00
 switchport port-security
 switchport port-security maximum 2
!
interface range GigabitEthernet0/13 - 22
 description UNUSED
 switchport mode access
 switchport access vlan 999
 shutdown
```

The port-security and storm-control lines are shown only to place them in context. Violation modes and sticky MAC addresses belong to the port-security lesson.

**What to know.** Layer 2 is often the least monitored layer, yet attacks here bypass firewalls entirely because they happen before any packet reaches a router. Many Layer 2 features leave evidence in switch logs that a SOC can collect: err-disable events from BPDU Guard, MAC flapping messages, port-security violations, native VLAN mismatch warnings, and STP topology change notifications. A sudden burst of topology changes or a root bridge change is worth investigating, because it can mean a rogue device or a failing link.

**What to ask.** Is this port supposed to be trunking? Did a root bridge change at an unexpected time? Which wall jack is behind the port that just went err-disabled? Do our switch logs reach a central collector, so these events are visible to the analyst on shift?

sections.heading: Worked Troubleshooting: Two Hosts in the Same VLAN Cannot Communicate
sections.content:
Scenario: PC-A is on SW1 port Gi0/1 and PC-B is on SW2 port Gi0/2. Both should be in VLAN 10 with addresses in the same subnet, but PC-A cannot ping PC-B. Other VLANs between the same switches work. Use a bottom-up method: link state, VLAN membership, trunk, MAC table.

**Step 1: Is each port in the right VLAN?**

```
SW1# show vlan brief
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/1, Gi0/3
20   ENGINEERING                      active    Gi0/5, Gi0/6

SW2# show vlan brief
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/2, Gi0/4
20   ENGINEERING                      active    Gi0/5
```

Both access ports are in VLAN 10, and VLAN 10 is active on both switches. Access configuration is fine, so the fault is in between.

**Step 2: Check the trunk.**

```
SW1# show interfaces trunk
Port        Mode         Encapsulation  Status        Native vlan
Gi0/24      on           802.1q         trunking      999

Port        Vlans allowed on trunk
Gi0/24      20,150

Port        Vlans in spanning tree forwarding state and not pruned
Gi0/24      20,150
```

The trunk is up, it uses 802.1Q, and the native VLAN is 999. But SW1 allows only VLANs 20 and 150, so VLAN 10 never leaves SW1 on this trunk (SW2's list still shows 10,20,150). That fits an engineer who ran switchport trunk allowed vlan 20,150 without the add keyword.

**Step 3: Confirm with the MAC tables.**

```
SW1# show mac address-table vlan 10
  10    0050.7966.6800    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1

SW2# show mac address-table vlan 10
  10    0050.7966.6801    DYNAMIC     Gi0/2
```

Each switch has learned only its local host in VLAN 10. PC-A's ARP request, a broadcast, was flooded in VLAN 10 on SW1 but never crossed the trunk, so PC-B never saw it and no reply came back.

**Step 4: Fix and verify.**

```
SW1(config)# interface GigabitEthernet0/24
SW1(config-if)# switchport trunk allowed vlan add 10
SW1(config-if)# end

SW1# show mac address-table vlan 10
  10    0050.7966.6800    DYNAMIC     Gi0/1
  10    0050.7966.6801    DYNAMIC     Gi0/24
```

After a ping succeeds, PC-B's MAC appears on the trunk port Gi0/24.

**Other causes with the same symptom.** The same three commands rule these out:

- **VLAN missing on one switch.** It is absent from the allowed-and-active block of show interfaces trunk and from show vlan brief. Create it.
- **Native VLAN mismatch.** Untagged traffic lands in different VLANs on each side, and the CDP mismatch log appears. Make both ends match.
- **STP blocking.** show spanning-tree vlan 10 reveals a blocked trunk.

**The takeaway.** Always compare both ends. Two correct-looking switches can disagree on a single list, and the show commands tell you exactly where.

quiz.question: A switch receives a frame in VLAN 10 whose destination MAC address is not in its MAC address table. What does it do with the frame?

options.label: Floods it out every other port that belongs to VLAN 10
Drops it and waits for the sender to retry after an ARP exchange
Sends it only through the uplink trunk toward the gateway
Floods it out every port on the switch, in all VLANs

quiz.explanation: Unknown unicast is flooded within the VLAN on which it arrived, excluding the ingress port, so the owner can receive it and reply, which lets the switch learn its location. Dropping the frame would break normal first-contact communication, because switches do not wait for ARP or retries. Forwarding only to the uplink assumes the switch knows where the destination is, and it does not. Flooding into other VLANs would destroy the isolation that VLANs provide.

quiz.question: A trunk carries VLANs 10, 20 and 150. An engineer types switchport trunk allowed vlan 30 on it to add VLAN 30. What is the result?

options.label: VLAN 30 is appended and the trunk carries 10, 20, 30 and 150
The command is rejected until the add keyword is supplied
The trunk now carries only VLAN 30, since the list was replaced
VLAN 30 is added but VLAN 150 is removed as the oldest entry

quiz.explanation: Without the add keyword the command overwrites the allowed list, so only VLAN 30 crosses the trunk and VLANs 10, 20 and 150 suddenly lose connectivity between switches. IOS does not append automatically, which is exactly why the add keyword exists. IOS also does not reject the command, since it is valid syntax that simply replaces the list. No oldest-entry removal logic exists, because the list is a plain set of VLAN numbers that you define in full.

quiz.question: A used switch from a test lab, in your VTP domain with a matching name, has configuration revision 85 and few VLANs. Production is at revision 40. It is connected by a trunk. What happens?

options.label: Production switches keep their VLANs because servers always override clients
Production switches adopt the lab database and missing VLANs are deleted
The databases are merged, so both sets of VLANs exist everywhere
Only VLANs with identical names are kept and all other VLANs are removed

quiz.explanation: VTP compares only the revision number. The higher revision wins and replaces the receiving switch's VLAN database completely, which deletes VLANs that the lab switch lacks and leaves their access ports inactive. Role does not matter, since clients advertise too, and a server does not override a higher revision coming from a client. VTP never merges databases. It also does not filter by VLAN name. Using transparent mode, or resetting the revision before connecting the switch, prevents this.

quiz.question: Access port Gi0/5 has PortFast and BPDU Guard enabled. A user plugs a small managed switch into the wall jack, and the port logs a BPDU Guard violation. What state is the port in?

options.label: It becomes root-inconsistent and stops forwarding only until the BPDUs end
It moves to blocking and returns to forwarding after 50 seconds
It stays up but discards the BPDUs and keeps forwarding user frames
It goes into err-disable and stays down until someone resets it

quiz.explanation: BPDU Guard puts the port into err-disable the moment a BPDU arrives on a PortFast port, and it stays down until an admin runs shutdown then no shutdown, or an errdisable recovery timer expires. Blocking for 50 seconds describes classic STP timers, not this protection. Silently discarding BPDUs is the behavior of BPDU filter, which hides the problem. Root-inconsistent is the Root Guard result, which recovers automatically when the superior BPDUs stop, so it does not match.

quiz.question: One switch configures channel-group 1 mode active on two uplinks, and the neighbor configures channel-group 1 mode on. What happens?

options.label: The bundle does not negotiate, because LACP and static mode cannot talk
The bundle forms because active mode falls back to static automatically
The bundle forms with only one member carrying traffic at a time
Both switches move to PAgP and the bundle forms after a few seconds

quiz.explanation: Mode active sends LACP packets, but mode on sends none and expects none, so the active side never sees a partner and keeps its ports stand-alone, while the static side may bundle on its own, which risks a loop. LACP has no automatic fallback to static unless a specific fallback feature is configured. The bundle does not form partially with a single active member. PAgP is a separate Cisco protocol and is never selected automatically when a switch is configured for LACP.
